title: Robust feedback control of collisional plasma dynamics in presence of uncertainties
abstract: Magnetic fusion aims to confine high-temperature plasma within a device, enabling the fusion of deuterium and tritium nuclei to release energy. Due to the very large temperatures involved, it is essential to isolate the plasma from the device walls to prevent structural damage and the external magnetic fields play a fundamental role in achieving this confinement. In realistic settings, the physical mechanisms governing plasma behavior are highly complex, involving numerous uncertain parameters and intricate particle interactions, such as collisions, that significantly affect both confinement efficiency and overall stability. In this work, we address particularly these challenges by proposing a robust feedback control strategy designed to steer the plasma towards a desired spatial region, despite the presence of uncertainties. From a modeling perspective, we consider a collisional plasma described by a Vlasov-Poisson-BGK system, which accounts for a self-consistent electric field and a strong external magnetic field, while incorporating uncertainty in the model. A key feature of the proposed control strategy is its independence from the random parameter, making it particularly suitable for practical applications. A series of numerical simulations confirms the effectiveness of our approach and demonstrates the ability of external magnetic fields to successfully confine plasma away from the device boundaries, even in the presence of uncertain conditions.

title: Structure and asymptotic preserving deep neural surrogates for uncertainty quantification in multiscale kinetic equations
abstract: The high dimensionality of kinetic equations with stochastic parameters poses major computational challenges for uncertainty quantification (UQ). Traditional Monte Carlo (MC) sampling methods, while widely used, suffer from slow convergence and high variance, which become increasingly severe as the dimensionality of the parameter space grows. To accelerate MC sampling, we adopt a multiscale control variates strategy that leverages low-fidelity solutions from simplified kinetic models to reduce variance. To further improve sampling efficiency and preserve the underlying physics, we introduce surrogate models based on structure and asymptotic preserving neural networks (SAPNNs). These deep neural networks are specifically designed to satisfy key physical properties, including positivity, conservation laws, entropy dissipation, and asymptotic limits. By training the SAPNNs on low-fidelity models and enriching them with selected high-fidelity samples from the full Boltzmann equation, our method achieves significant variance reduction while maintaining physical consistency and asymptotic accuracy. The proposed methodology enables efficient large-scale prediction in kinetic UQ and is validated across both homogeneous and nonhomogeneous multiscale regimes. Numerical results demonstrate improved accuracy and computational efficiency compared to standard MC techniques.

title: Control strategies for magnetized plasma: a polar coordinates framework
abstract: In this work, we provide an overview of various control strategies aimed at steering plasma toward desired configurations using an external magnetic field. From a modeling perspective, we focus on the Vlasov equation in a two-dimensional bounded domain, accounting for both a self-induced electric field and a strong external magnetic field. The results are presented in a polar coordinate framework, which is particularly well-suited for simulating toroidal devices such as Tokamaks and Stellarators. A key feature of the proposed control strategies is their feedback mechanism, which is based on an instantaneous prediction of the discretized system. Finally, different numerical experiments in the two-dimensional polar coordinate setting demonstrate the effectiveness of the approaches.

title: Micro-Macro Tensor Neural Surrogates for Uncertainty Quantification in Collisional Plasma
abstract: Plasma kinetic equations exhibit pronounced sensitivity to microscopic perturbations in model parameters and data, making reliable and efficient uncertainty quantification (UQ) essential for predictive simulations. However, the cost of uncertainty sampling, the high-dimensional phase space, and multiscale stiffness pose severe challenges to both computational efficiency and error control in traditional numerical methods. These aspects are further emphasized in presence of collisions where the high-dimensional nonlocal collision integrations and conservation properties pose severe constraints. To overcome this, we present a variance-reduced Monte Carlo framework for UQ in the Vlasov--Poisson--Landau (VPL) system, in which neural network surrogates replace the multiple costly evaluations of the Landau collision term. The method couples a high-fidelity, asymptotic-preserving VPL solver with inexpensive, strongly correlated surrogates based on the Vlasov--Poisson--Fokker--Planck (VPFP) and Euler--Poisson (EP) equations. For the surrogate models, we introduce a generalization of the separable physics-informed neural network (SPINN), developing a class of tensor neural networks based on an anisotropic micro-macro decomposition, to reduce velocity-moment costs, model complexity, and the curse of dimensionality. To further increase correlation with VPL, we calibrate the VPFP model and design an asymptotic-preserving SPINN whose small- and large-Knudsen limits recover the EP and VP systems, respectively. Numerical experiments show substantial variance reduction over standard Monte Carlo, accurate statistics with far fewer high-fidelity samples, and lower wall-clock time, while maintaining robustness to stochastic dimension.

title: Full-horizon magnetic control of the Vlasov--Poisson system for plasma confinement
abstract: We study the full-horizon control of a two-dimensional Vlasov--Poisson system through an externally imposed magnetic field. The control is represented by time-dependent coefficients associated with smooth, spatially localized basis functions, and is designed to steer selected position and velocity moments of the distribution function while limiting particle dispersion and the control effort. Starting from the kinetic constrained optimization problem, we derive the continuous first-order optimality conditions, including a backward Vlasov equation, an elliptic adjoint equation, and the variational inequality associated with bounded controls. We then project this system onto a particle--grid representation and identify the resulting particle adjoints and control gradient. The full-horizon field is then computed on a reduced particle ensemble, initialized by an instantaneous control, and subsequently applied to a larger set of particles. Numerical experiments indicate that the instantaneous control field already provides an effective baseline, while the full-horizon correction can further reduce the relative thermal energy near the boundaries and improve confinement over the prescribed time interval.

title: A Riemann-invariant contact-capturing scheme with WENO reconstruction and RH-motivated dual-speed dissipation for compressible two-phase mixture flows
abstract: This work develops and benchmarks centred (Riemann-solver-free) finite-volume fluxes for a hyperbolic two-phase mixture model with velocity non-equilibrium. The baseline method combines a Riemann-invariant contact-capturing algorithm (RICCA) with dual-speed dissipation and primitive-variable WENO3/WENO5 reconstruction, avoiding full eigen-decomposition while retaining a conservative update. An RH-motivated companion flux (RICCA--RH) is introduced, in which the acoustic weight in $\alpha = |V_n| + Ba$ is controlled by a binary pressure/Rankine--Hugoniot switch. On one-dimensional gas--magma Riemann suite, RICCA--RH tracks legacy RICCA and is sharper than first-order FORCE/Lax--Friedrichs at material contacts; a linearised spectral study clarifies how its dual-speed dissipation differs from FORCE. With WENO5, RICCA, RICCA--RH and FORCE produce essentially identical smooth profiles, indicating that most differences are confined to first-order contact metrics. In two dimensions (gas--liquid benchmarks), the production flux implemented on CPU and Apple Metal reproduces expansion-tube, collision and forward-facing-step patterns and yields intermediate cut-based roughness between RICCA and FORCE. High order is obtained using an approximate face-normal acoustic characteristic reconstruction, a pragmatic multi-variable hybrid sensor, and a Zhang--Shu-style invariant-domain face limiter on $(\rho,\alpha,c)$. An under-dissipative soft-switch variant that rings severely is also documented, and a resident 2D Metal kernel on Apple Silicon is reported to deliver up to $3.9\times$ wall-clock speedup on completed CPU/Metal comparisons (peak on the $101\times101$ expansion tube).

title: Multicomponent Adaptive Sampling Configuration Interaction method in openLOWDIN: positronic and quantum nuclear systems
abstract: We present a multicomponent Selective Configuration Interaction (SCI) method based on the deterministic Adaptive Sampling CI (ASCI) algorithm for computing energies and wavefunction properties of molecular systems containing leptons of variable masses, or quantum nuclei. Near-FCI accuracy is achieved by incorporating second-order Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory or by dressing the Hamiltonian via Davidson's and co-workers shifted-Bk method. We validate the approach through benchmark positronic (e$^+$LiH, e$^+$OH$^-$, e$^+$Mg) and quantum nuclear systems (HCN), establishing a novel protocol for accurate convergence, based on the iterative adaptation of natural orbitals starting from those obtained by considering only cross-particle CISD excitations, to those obtained from SCI variational space, surpassing the accuracy of previous SCI studies. Overall, we show that the present multi-component SCI framework offers a simple, systematically improvable, and cost-effective alternative to traditional CI approaches.

title: Symmetry-reduced k-point sampling and Wannier analysis with localized Gaussian orbitals
abstract: Brillouin-zone sampling with localized orbitals requires consistent transformations between sparse real-space matrices and complex Bloch states. Symmetry reduces the number of reciprocal-space problems, but scalar integration weights alone cannot reconstruct the matrices and wavefunctions needed for densities and orbital analysis. We develop a unified formulation of these transformations for nonorthogonal Gaussian bases and describe its implementation in CP2K. Atom permutations, local orbital rotations, and lattice phases connect irreducible-point solutions to full symmetry orbits while preserving the overlap metric. Direct and fast lattice transforms couple this construction to self-consistent calculations, including complex orbital optimization and finite-temperature occupations. Gauge-consistent full-mesh orbitals and directed inter-point overlaps support Wannier90 export, Wannier construction, and Hamiltonian interpolation. In silicon and aluminium tests, symmetry reduces a 64-point mesh to four representatives while retaining cell energies or electronic free energies within $1.5\times10^{-12}$ hartree of the unreduced calculation. Hybrid exchange and many-body applications illustrate the additional role of auxiliary bases and transfer momenta. The resulting framework connects symmetry-reduced integration to gauge-consistent analysis of periodic electronic states within a localized-orbital representation.

title: High-Order Regularization for Singular and Nearly Singular Laplace and Stokes Layer Potentials in Two Dimensions
abstract: Layer potentials represent the solutions of many elliptic boundary value problems, but their kernels have the singularity of the fundamental solution, so standard quadrature loses accuracy at targets on or near the boundary. In two dimensions, Gaussian regularization of the logarithmic kernel gives a smooth kernel involving the exponential integral $E_1$, but for the single layer its regularization error is only first order in the smoothing radius $\delta$. We construct modified kernels for two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes single- and double-layer potentials that achieve regularization error $O(\delta^p)$, $p=3,5,7$, uniformly for targets on and near the curve. The resulting method is both high-order accurate and easy to implement: the integrals are evaluated directly by the periodic trapezoidal rule on a single fixed set of boundary nodes for all targets. Choosing $\delta=c h^q$ with $q<1$, where $h$ is the node spacing, keeps the discretization error smaller than the regularization error as $h\to0$, and numerical experiments confirm the predicted $O(h^{pq})$ convergence. Finally, we combine the near-curve evaluation with a fast Poisson solver to compute the potentials on the entire Cartesian grid.

title: Constitutive-fibre mechanics: mechanics-directed uncertainty in constitutive function space
abstract: A structural prediction rests on constitutive functions that are known only through a finite number of tests. The tests fix the response along the states they visit; together with a declared regularity bound they leave a set of admissible constitutive functions, which we call the constitutive fibre. Constitutive-fibre mechanics (CFM) computes the range of a quantity of interest over this set. Adjoint solves of the mechanical problem represent the test observations and the quantity of interest as elements of the constitutive function space. The part of the sensitivity of the quantity of interest that is orthogonal to all observation sensitivities is hidden from the tests; for exact data it alone determines the half-width of the prediction, and for data with tolerance the half-width is a finite convex problem in the span of the adjoint representers. Comparing the two values shows whether a new type of test or a more precise test is needed, and a rank-one update ranks candidate tests before they are performed. A learned constitutive class can only under-represent the range; the deficit is computable. Beyond the linear range, an optimality system with state-dependent representers gives the extreme constitutive functions. The same set decides whether the prediction is defined for every admissible constitutive function, which is a different question from its precision. For a phase-field bar with unknown degradation function, 3% of the sensitivity of the stability eigenvalue is hidden and produces 70% of its uncertainty. For an open-hole composite lamina, the coupon that sharpens the compliance most is not the one that makes the prediction valid; validity is proved on a declared cell by a certificate accepted in exact arithmetic.

title: Development and Validation of a preCICE Based OpenMOC OpenFOAM Coupling Framework for Nuclear Reactor Analysis
abstract: To address the long computation time required by stochastic solvers, which are applied in the coupled neutronics-thermal hydraulics (N-TH) calculations, a faster N-TH coupling framework is developed based on the multiphysics coupling library preCICE, which enables data exchange between OpenMOC and OpenFOAM. As an alternative to commonly used stochastic solvers, like OpenMC, OpenMOC is used as a neutronics solver providing much faster steady-state solution in a Picard iteration. To realize this coupling strategy, OpenMC is used for an initial one-time computation cost for multi-group cross sections data generation that is used throughout OpenMOC calculations. A preCICE library adapter for OpenMOC is also developed, allowing data exchange between neutronic power distributions and thermal hydraulic temperature fields. Our proposed coupling framework is validated through simulations of a simplified 2 times 2 fuel assembly, and a quartered geometry of 17 times 17 fuel assembly. The comparison shows good agreement with established referenced solutions, highlighting our proposed coupling framework for the steady-state N-TH coupling at a fraction of the time required by stochastic solver codes. This advantages could be extended for future applications where fast approximated solutions are required to address the change of N-TH coupling due to small parametric changes like in digital twin of nuclear reactor.

title: Orbital differentiation in a rare earth ion near half filling
abstract: In the electronic structure of rare earth ions, details can be crucial for understanding the origin of correlated states. Currently, state-of-the-art wavefunction-based methods (e.g. CASSCF) can capture single-ion properties of molecular magnets and some band insulating systems, but are expensive to perform, and cannot be applied to metallic systems. Here, we carry out full multiplet calculations for SmN with the cubic rock-salt structure using the crystal field software Quanty. The calculated experimental observables from our model agree precisely with magnetic susceptibility and inelastic neutron scattering experiments, and the spatially resolved spin density also agrees with DFT predictions. By tuning the crystal field parameters, our full multiplet-derived wavefunctions reveal the presence of orbital differentiation of the ground $J=\frac{5}{2}$ manifold into two groups, which are distinct subspaces with different orbital stiffness. This violation of Hund's rule, observed with a fast and inexpensive calculation tool, represents a step forward for microscopic models of rare earth materials, and may provide support for the claim of unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.

title: A branchless single-precision Voigt approximation for spectral synthesis
abstract: The Voigt function is evaluated repeatedly in spectral synthesis, and several widely used implementations carry an absolute error floor. We construct QLG, a family of branchless, single-precision approximations, separable in the damping parameter $a$. QLG is named for its three ingredients: Lorentzian and Gaussian generators $L$ and $G$, and an envelope $q$ that multiplies every fitted correction and vanishes at both endpoints. The leading Lorentzian wing amplitude is fixed analytically. Three members reach observed maximum full-profile relative errors of $6.5\times10^{-3}$, $9.2\times10^{-4}$, and $7\times10^{-5}$ over $a\in[10^{-9},10^{9}]$ and $|v|\le10^{5}$. Extended-domain and randomized checks support these error levels. For the tested SIU, MOOG, and Humlicek w4 implementations, the relative error instead approaches 100% towards small values of the damping parameter. We compare synthesis-weighted costs on an Apple M1 and an AMD EPYC 9554 using gfortran 15, and propagate errors through solar-dwarf, red-supergiant, and M-dwarf syntheses. The least expensive member costs 0.98-1.05 times as much as the tabulated Synspec kernel on the M1 and 1.11-1.20 times as much on the EPYC, with a maximum flux error smaller by a factor of 3.6. The intermediate member costs less than every tested arithmetic kernel and holds the flux error below $10^{-3}$. The most accurate member costs 1.6-3.0 times less than w4 and gives 3.4-5.0 times smaller maximum flux errors in the tested syntheses.

title: Burgers vectors from Voronoi topology
abstract: Automated dislocation analysis is standard in atomistic simulations, yet current tools are limited to a handful of crystal structures. We introduce an algorithm without adjustable parameters, based on Voronoi topology, that identifies dislocations in a broad class of crystals. Each face shared by two cells that match the ideal crystal is taken as a step in it, and summing these steps around closed circuits of such cells yields exact Burgers vectors, without geometric templates. Tested on dislocations inserted into all 9,610 Materials Project structures whose Voronoi cells are stable with a wide margin, the algorithm finds every dislocation with its correct Burgers vector. In raw molecular-dynamics snapshots, including eleven dislocation types in $\theta$-Al$_2$Cu and bcc iron up to its melting point, every Burgers vector it returns is correct, although near melting the dislocations merge into one cluster. Voronoi topology thus provides a natural language in which a crystal, its defects, and their Burgers vectors are all described.

title: Coordinating integration of multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation codes with design structure matrices
abstract: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.

title: A variational multiscale rotational pressure-correction method for incompressible flows with open boundaries
abstract: Rotational pressure correction improves pressure accuracy near open boundaries in incompressible flow simulations, but equal-order finite element discretizations can still develop spurious pressure oscillations. We develop a residual-based variational multiscale rotational pressure-correction scheme (RPCS-VMS) that stabilizes both the pressure-increment and pressure-recovery equations. By constructing stage-specific momentum residuals using a common intermediate-velocity acceleration, the scheme retains four sequential linear solves per time step. For a reduced BDF1 Oseen model with frozen stabilization coefficients, we establish augmented-energy decay and a conditional bound on the pressure gradient. Manufactured-solution tests demonstrate suppression of pressure oscillations at small time steps and reduced near-boundary pressure errors. With \(P_1/P_1\) and \(Q_1/Q_1\) elements, the observed spatial \(L^2\) convergence rates are 2 for velocity and approximately \(1.5\) for pressure, while first- and second-order backward differentiation formulas attain their expected temporal orders. Branched-pipe and two- and three-dimensional cylinder benchmarks assess outlet flow partitioning, transient forces, and pressure differences, with results agreeing closely with reference solutions. In the three-dimensional cylinder test, RPCS-VMS achieves a 2.41-fold wall-time speedup over the tested monolithic VMS solver.

title: Non-Intrusive Rubin Substructuring for Geometrically Nonlinear Structures via Nonlinear Manifolds
abstract: Component mode synthesis enables modular reduction of large structural models, but its extension to geometrically nonlinear systems remains challenging. This work generalizes the Rubin method by introducing a cubic displacement manifold that statically condenses high-frequency free-interface modes onto the retained low-frequency modes and residual attachment modes. The reduced equations of motion, with cubic polynomial restoring forces, are derived by Galerkin projection onto the manifold tangent subspace. The consistency of the reduced forces is guaranteed by the cubic expansion of the component-level reduced manifold. We further present a non-intrusive procedure that combines elastic-force identification with finite-difference estimates of tangent-stiffness derivatives, which allows the reduced model to be constructed from the linear Rubin model and tangent-stiffness evaluations. In the proposed numerical tests, the reduced assembled models accurately reproduce the nonlinear responses of the full finite-element models, including internal resonance and modal coupling. Scalability and significant computational gains are demonstrated with an industrial scale model of a wing-box tip tank assembly, for which an online speed-up of about 24,666 was obtained.

title: Quadrature-Free Radial Intracule Densities: A Bessel-Harmonic Formulation for Gaussian Basis Sets
abstract: The radial intracule density $I(R)$, the probability distribution of the interelectronic distance, is a compact and physically transparent picture of electron correlation, but its evaluation for molecules has always relied on a numerical angular quadrature over the orientation of the interelectronic vector. We show that this quadrature can be removed altogether for Cartesian Gaussian basis sets and arbitrary second-order density matrices. Starting from the Hermite Gaussian expansion of the products of basis functions, the coupling exponential $e^{2\mu\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{T}}$ that links radial and angular variables is expanded in modified spherical Bessel functions and real spherical harmonics, and the expansion terminates rigorously at $l=p_x+p_y+p_z$, where the $p$'s are the Cartesian powers arising from the Hermite expansion. The angular average is then exact, the atomic limit reduces to a finite sum of terms $C_iR^{n_i}e^{-\mu R^2}$, and the radial moments $\int_0^\infty R^nI(R)\,dR$ are given in closed form through the confluent hypergeometric function ${}_1F_1$. The scheme is exact in principle and fails only arithmetically: we identify the catastrophic cancellations in the angular-momentum coupling that ruin binary64 evaluations for heavy atoms and remove them by elevating the cancelling chain to binary128. Sum rules for the total, Coulomb and exchange-correlation intracules are recovered to seven to eight significant digits for systems from LiH to Kr$_2$, whereas Euler-Maclaurin and Lebedev quadratures err by up to 22% for stretched or multicenter molecules.

title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
abstract: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

title: A free-energy approach for stochastic reaction-drift-diffusion lattice simulations of crowded biological systems
abstract: Molecular size alters spatial distributions, reaction equilibria, and transport in crowded mixtures, but resolving individual particle encounters can make large stochastic simulations computationally costly. We developed a lattice-based framework for simulating reaction-drift-diffusion systems with volume exclusion captured as a free energy functional in each voxel. Changes in this free energy, together with external one-body potentials, modify diffusion and reaction propensities. Our framework accommodates mixtures of particle sizes without resolving each particle's position within a voxel. We implemented our framework in an operator splitting scheme and compared our predictions with off-lattice interacting-particle simulations. Inclusion of the local free energy functional improved spatial occupancies and shifts in reaction equilibria relative to point-particle simulations. With separate approximations for larger spheres and polymers, we simulated crowding-induced slowing and spatial segregation. We then modeled motor proteins' traffic jams on a structured track representing a microtubule. Our results demonstrate how local composition can inform stochastic reaction and transport rates without resolving individual encounters.

title: Right shape, wrong time: phase errors of ODE solvers in the flame problem
abstract: The flame model $y'=y^2-y^3$, $y(0)=\delta$, is a standard illustration of stiffness: for $\delta=10^{-4}$ the stiff MATLAB solvers ode23s and ode15s need only 99 and 140 steps, against 3040 for ode45. We show that these cheap solutions have the right shape at the wrong time: they place the front 29 and 329 time units early, with maximal errors 0.95 and 1.00. Because all solutions are time translates of one master profile, the global error of every numerical solution with values in $[\delta,1)$ is exactly a phase error, $y_k=y_\delta(t_k-D_k)$. For fixed-step one-step methods of order $p$ we prove $D=h^p\int_\delta^{y}g+O(h^{p+1})$ with a remainder bounded uniformly in $\delta$, so that the delay grows at most like $h\ln(1/\delta)$ for $p=1$ and stays bounded for $p\geq2$. For any computed solution the delay is exactly the sum of its defects with respect to the exact flow, converted into time; a heuristic model, confirmed by MATLAB runs, explains why it is created in the first few steps and why tightening the tolerances is an expensive cure. Integrating for $1/y$, which runs like a clock in the slow phase, with an absolute tolerance reduces the error by several orders of magnitude, at a median cost close to that of the standard formulation. The mechanism needs only that the equation is autonomous; its general form is the subject of a companion paper.

title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators
abstract: Substantial challenges in physics-informed learning have motivated many improvements, but fragmented implementations hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison. We propose OpenPINN/PINO, an extensible open-source PyTorch framework for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Two shared specifications connect problem setup, local computation, and evaluation. Agents support problem formulation, solver planning, and diagnosis. ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data. MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register new problem templates and method components, then combine or compare strategies such as Fourier features, residual-adaptive sampling, and self-adaptive loss weighting for a fixed problem. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, and propose solver plans. The framework validates these specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code. A diagnostic agent reviews training logs and evaluation results to identify problems and suggest revisions. Three examples show how method choices and agent diagnostics affect accuracy. For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative $L^2$ error by about $75\%$ from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative $L^2$ error by about $68\%$ across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization. After initial training failure, all three runs met the $10\%$ target, with relative $L^2$ displacement errors of $3.51\%$--$6.31\%$.
